newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway PM talked to KGB during Cold War--report.
newsitem.headline: Norway PM talked to KGB during Cold War--report.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland, now Norway's prime minister, had regular talks as a "discussion partner" with the Soviet KGB during the Cold War, news reports said on Tuesday.

Norwegian dailies Verdens Gang and Dagbladet said Jagland was code-named "Juri" by the Soviet intelligence agency, whose diplomat agents in Oslo discussed politics with him in his role as leader of the Labour Party's Youth League in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Verdens Gang quoted Jagland as saying that it was part of his job at the time to keep in touch with foreign embassies, including Soviet diplomats, and that he notified the Labour Party of his contacts.
"It was part of the Labour Party's policy to inform as much as possible about the political situation in Norway in order for the Soviet Union not to misunderstand anything," Jagland said.
NATO member Norway shares an Arctic border with Russia.
The reports, to be detailed in a documentary on Norwegian NRK television on Tuesday night, came in the middle of campaigning for Norway's September 15 election.
"The newspaper headlines will not lead to a change in the party's election campaign strategy," Jagland told the national news agency NTB.

Opinion polls suggest that Jagland's Labour minority government, which is seeking to defend a tight fiscal policy against opposition demands for more public spending on health care, could suffer a major setback in the election.
Norway's intelligence police said they had never had reason to launch an investigation into Jagland's activities during the Cold War.
"We have no information that would indicate that Jagland had irregular contact with representatives for a foreign power," a police spokesman told NTB.
Dagbladet said Jagland and two other named Norwegian Labour politicians "were not looked upon as spies (by the KGB), but they were used as interesting and knowledgeable discussion partners".
